subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `Bundle` copies the `*Capture` pointer and releases the lock before `BuildBundle` streams the spill files, while `StartCollect`, `runCollect` and eviction all call `Capture.Close()` (which blanks `SpillPath` and `os.RemoveAll`s the directory). Unsynchronised field write plus real evidence loss: the vendor bundle gets a one-line placeholder where a 50 MB tech-support file should be, and `SHA256SUMS` hashes the stub.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `HandleClassify` and `HandlePlan` call `Resolve(w, r, false)`, so they run at `infrastructure:read`. The built-in Read-only role ("View everything, change nothing") can null another operator's prepared plan, and at the 64-escalation bound can evict a finished collection and delete its spill directory. Every sibling handler in the same file deliberately takes the write gate.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `seen[intent]` is set at the top of the closure, so the guard that files an out-of-bounds probe as `Unbound` is dead. The intent vanishes from both `Steps` and `Unbound`, and the plan's own coverage sentence can then claim every command is authored. Reachable whenever a class binds `ping {peer}` and the incident carries no peer.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `parseBlockScalar` fixes the indent base from the first body line and never re-floors it, so a later, less-indented body line yields `strings.Repeat(" ", negative)` and panics. Reproduced. Reachable from the customer capture-upload route (`infrastructure:write`); net/http contains it per connection, so the cost is a dropped connection plus a stack trace per request instead of the refusal every other malformed upload gets.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `c.client.StagingHost` is written on the shared vendor client outside any lock and read later inside the retry closure. Data race, and one tenant's onboarding staging host can receive another tenant's production case. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `attachOnlyMissingFields` demands an upload token from every attach-only connector, but the email transport never reads one, so the `email-cisco` route can never submit. The package's own design-doc-backed required-field table says the SR number alone is sufficient.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `LookupCaseNumber` returns the newest vendor reply in the mailbox with nothing tying it to the case being polled, so two unnumbered cases to the same vendor both get the same case number. A real Graph read failure is also collapsed into `ErrCapabilityUnsupported`.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The S3 endpoint host is concatenated from vendor-supplied `bucket` and `region` with no charset check and no `amazonaws.com` pinning, so `/`, `#` or `?` reparents the PUT. Needs a compromised vendor gateway, so this is defence in depth, and Cisco's `cxdBase` shows the pattern that should have been copied. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `tacCandidateExport` is the only hand-rolled fetch in the file that omits `X-Acting-Tenant`, so the Knowledge export writes a different tenant's candidates than the list beside it, and always 400s for the platform owner.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The per-case reset effect is keyed on `corrId`, which is `""` for described investigations. Switching between two of them leaves the previous case's TAC chip and Iris answer on screen, and the chip's Refresh posts against the new incident id.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The CXD upload token is declared, cleared and sent, but no input ever sets it. The server therefore always blocks an attach-only Cisco route, and the blocker's settings hint matches no route, so it renders as inert text pointing at a field that does not exist.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: Queued / Failed / Delivered are counted over one page of 50 outbox rows, and both stores page oldest-first with no purge, so recent failures are structurally outside the sample. "Failed 0" while deliveries are dead-lettering.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The reviewed-command allow set is registered under a bare device key with no refcount, so a second escalation on the same device overwrites it and then deletes it on its own `ErrCollectBusy` exit. Fails closed (commands refused, never widened) and the refusal is recorded on the capture row.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `Confirm` checks only that a proposal exists. `StartCollect` nils the capture without clearing the proposal, so a case can be opened naming no device.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `PersistCase` runs on the client's request context after the vendor case already exists, so a disconnect loses the durable link. `fileLearning` in the same package already uses `context.WithoutCancel` for exactly this hazard.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: `PutRecord`'s rollback restores a slice header over an array the in-place sort already permuted, so a flush failure keeps the record it reports as failed and drops the oldest one.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: DELETE maps every store error to 404, so a failed write reads as "already gone" with no audit row and no log. The PUT arm in the same handler splits the cases correctly. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The documented 1000-invocations-per-hour budget is counted on the shared client, so it is enforced across all tenants combined against a per-customer vendor ceiling. Fails closed, self-heals in an hour. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: The incident-to-correlation bridge compares `SourceType == "correlation"`, a value `normalizeSourceType` can never store, so the branch is dead and the missing correlation evidence is not recorded in `Missing` either.

subsystem: 3.1 TAC escalation and vendor case handling
what: Over-long and over-cap `log_signatures` are dropped with a bare `continue`, so a detection regex the research pass added silently never exists while the report prints zero refusals. Every other rejection in the file goes through `Report.refuse`.

`RecordChange`'s rollback aliases the slice `trimChanges` sorted in place, so a failed disk write keeps the change it just reported as failed and drops the oldest persisted one, then flushes that state on the next success. Reproduced by probe.

`severityFor` treats a MISSING reliability grade as trustworthy, so the flaky-synthetic severity cap never fires for an ungraded check, which is the default state. Collecting more evidence then *lowers* the severity. Journey-scoped entities never key into the map at all, so the cap is bypassed for every journey incident.

`ListChanges` pushes only the time bound into SQL and applies type/app/site filters in Go after `LIMIT 500`, so a filtered query on a busy tenant can answer "No change was recorded in this window" while the deploy that caused the incident sits one page down. The file backend filters first, so the two backends disagree.

An unreadable store file is folded into the absent case: empty store, `loadErr` nil, nothing logged. The first write then renames a temp file over the original, destroying every tenant's journeys, changes and promotions (or the target catalogue). Needs only a writable directory.
`JourneyForm` is rendered without a `key`, so switching from editing journey A to journey B reuses the instance and saves A's name, SLO, value and full step graph over B.
The change list is read at the 500 cap and then reports `total`, `complete` and `X-Total-Count` from that truncated set, so a caller asking for 500 is told the answer is complete.
The journey GET maps every store error to 404, so a database outage reads as a deleted journey. The PUT and DELETE arms split the cases correctly.
Same shape on the target GET: any store failure becomes a silent 404, with no log and no counter.

`Cohort`'s eight free-text dimensions are the only wire fields never clipped, on the operator change route and on the ingest route whose credential the code says must be assumed public. `MaxCohortDimensionsLen` is declared and referenced nowhere.

The DEM flow endpoint key is `addr:port` split on the FIRST colon, so every IPv6 subject's flow evidence fails `Atoi` and is dropped with no counter and no log. The passive-flow anchor then never fires.
`Run` returns on context cancel without draining `q.ch`, so queued batches are discarded with no `EventsDropped` increment and no log. HTTP shutdown runs first, so the window is small.

`metricHelp` names 9 of 15 counters, so ingest refusals, rejections and promotion errors can never be rendered. In any case nothing calls `Counters.Write`: the whole block reaches no surface. (both lenses)

`Validate` places no upper bound on `StartedAt`, and pruning is decided from the newest run's timestamp, so a far-future record pins its ring and permanently consumes one of the 5000 definition slots.

When every target is paused, `scored == 0` and the response-level reason is overwritten with `no_prober`, telling the operator to debug a prober that is working. `ReasonPaused` exists and is used per row.

The per-tenant target cap is a `SELECT count(*)` outside any lock at READ COMMITTED, with no constraint behind it, so two concurrent creates can both take the last slot. The comment claims the opposite.

The Postgres catalogue is the default backend and has no isolation test: the rule-5 test builds `NewFileStore`. Its scoped statements carry no tenant predicate and rest entirely on FORCE-RLS, which is correct today but unguarded against regression.

An over-cap tenant bucket is truncated at load with a bare `break` and no `loadErr`, so the excess targets are silently unmeasured and the next write persists the truncation. `ImportFile` refuses the same condition loudly.

`FetchDEMRuns` folds a transport error into the expired-key branch, so a broken connection returns an empty batch with a nil error. The drain counts nothing, logs nothing, and every check grades `unknown`.

Every read carries `?timeout=20s`, which makes OpenSearch return 200 with `timed_out: true` and partial aggregations. `osResponse` decodes the flag and nobody reads it; `_shards.failed` is not decoded at all. Posture, coverage, facets, trend and compliance scores are then computed from a partial fold and presented as complete, with `truncated` false because the total shrank with the buckets. (both lenses)

The detection window is `[now - interval, now]` recomputed per pass, while the real spacing is jittered interval plus scan duration. Every tick leaves a gap, and a skipped tick or a restart leaves the whole outage unassessed, with no finding, no UNASSESSED verdict and no log.

The Detections tab fetches the newest 200 current findings of *all* lanes and filters to the threat lane in the browser, ignoring `next_cursor`. A posture scan burst pushes real detections off the page and the screen prints "No detection fired in this window."
The "Why no verdict" panel requests unassessed findings with no limit (server default 100) and prints each grouped reason as "N controls". A 1,400-control credential outage renders as 100.

A control whose only finding is `Unknown` is counted into `Assessed`, excluded from `Unassessed`, scores null, and is then described by a note saying no control was assessed. The frameworks panel prints both numbers together.

When every matched index reports no size (closed or relocating), the empty-bucket branch returns a MEASURED zero with the detail "the pattern matched no index", dropping the `sizeless` caveat it computed. The mixed case is handled correctly.

`HandleStatus` scopes the tenant rows and then serves `metrics.Snapshot()` unfiltered: platform-wide scan runs, per-class emission counts, dead-letter and lost totals, to any `administration:write` holder. An aggregate inference channel, not a row leak. (both lenses)

Cross-tenant rule state is folded last-writer-wins over an unordered map (and an unordered SQL read), so the platform view of a rule flips between refreshes when two tenants disagree. The framework register does the same fold with an explicit union and says so.

`DeleteView` casts a caller-supplied id with `$1::uuid` while the handler validates only `isSafeToken`, so a non-UUID id answers 502 with the raw SQLSTATE text on Postgres and 404 on the file backend. (both lenses)
"N scored seams" prints the sum of per-seam finding counts, not the number of seams. The committed snapshot bakes the wrong number in.
A lane's rows are filtered client-side out of the first 100 findings while its badge count comes from the server-side facet, so a card can read "12 current" above "No verdicts yet."

The SR Linux weak-password regex allows exactly one token between `authentication` and `password`, so it only ever sees the two built-in users. Every configured list user is unexamined, and the detector still returns a clean verdict claiming all locally stored passwords are hashed.

`Match` traces any record carrying a well-formed `cx_debug=` marker with no check that the platform minted it, no rate limit and no arm requirement. An unauthenticated SNMP trap (community mismatch only drops device attribution) can therefore flush an operator's in-flight debug ring. Feature-flagged off by default.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: `checkPeers` computes `down` as `State == "down"` and treats everything else as up, so the documented third state `unknown` (which `bmp.Store.Close` sets for every peer of a closed session) dispatches "BGP peer X on Y is back up" and closes the incident. The vanished-peer case two lines below is handled correctly.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The peer recovery branch never deletes the cool-down stamp, unlike `resolveAlert`. A peer that flaps down again inside the 60-minute window produces no notification and no evidence record, only a counter.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: `ParseBGPState` (the primary AS-path source) drops an unreadable path element and joins the survivors, fabricating an AS adjacency and reporting full coverage. The sibling looking-glass parser marks the hop and the graph drops the path, and a test pins that behaviour.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The ASPA provider's transport error is wrapped verbatim, and Go's `*url.Error` carries the full URL including any query-string credential. `handleBGPASPA` returns it in a 200 body to any `infrastructure:read` caller, while `ASPAStatus` deliberately publishes only the hostname because the URL "may carry a token".

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The post-DNS SSRF dial gate is skipped whenever `ALL_PROXY` is set, but `http.ProxyFromEnvironment` never reads `ALL_PROXY`, so the request is dialled direct with no address check. `SafeOutboundURL` screens IP literals only, so a hostname resolving to an internal address passes.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The accept loop retries only on `net.Error` with `Timeout()`, and no deadline is ever set, so that branch is dead. Any other accept error (EMFILE under fd exhaustion) logs one warning and returns; the deferred shutdown closes the listener for the process lifetime while the API keeps reporting `receiver_enabled: true` and telling the operator to configure a router. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The BMP feed applies no operator-visibility restriction. `restrictedTelemetry` / `operatorTelemetryRestriction` are consulted nowhere in the package, so a platform owner reads an OperatorRestricted tenant's peers, AS paths and prefixes where logs, flows, metrics and igpmon all serve nothing.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The IPv6 architecture rule tests the network address only, so `::/0` is reported as an unallocated bogon. `0.0.0.0/0` correctly is not, so the two families disagree, and for a tenant watching `::/0` it raises a high-severity incident.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: A feed truncated at 20,000 entries (and every unparsable row) is stored as a clean refresh: entries reported, error empty, no truncation field, and no retry for the 6-hour TTL. Needs a non-default feed URL.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: `prefixWithinAny` uses `Overlaps`, which is symmetric, so a supernet row such as `0.0.0.0/0,KP` published in a discovered third-party feed is kept and rendered for the queried resource. The function's own doc and the file's trust posture both promise containment. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: `Stats` recomputes oldest and newest sequence by walking every session's full ring under the store mutex (the same lock the receive goroutines need), on all three read endpoints, for two values the ring can answer in O(1). Bounded at about 22 ms worst case.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: The globally monotonic `seq` is published in every row and in `next_cursor`, so a tenant can measure other tenants' update volume by differencing. `handleStats` deliberately withholds exactly that.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: A whitespace-only per-prefix key files the validation error under the untrimmed key while the panel reads the trimmed one, so Save silently does nothing forever with no visible error.

subsystem: 3.4 BGP: watch, depth, BMP, ops surface
what: Six new BGP panels and `RcaVerdictFeedback` render `e.message`, so the raw `502 Bad Gateway: {"error":"Get http://victoriametrics:8428/...: dial tcp 172.18.0.9:8428: connect: connection refused"}` envelope reaches the operator. `operatorError()` exists and is used by `AlertPolicyPanel` in the same directory.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `FileStore.SetGolden` clears the existing golden mark while scanning and only then discovers the requested version does not exist, so a 404 (an unknown sha, a pruned one, or a failed-capture row whose synthetic sha passes validation) leaves the device with no baseline. The Postgres backend rolls back.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `insertLocked` replaces a matching row wholesale with a freshly built `Version` whose `Golden` is false, so reverting a device to its golden configuration and re-capturing it clears the golden mark. The Postgres `ON CONFLICT` list omits the column and is unaffected.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The MTU/BW/speed/duplex scan runs on every line of an interface record including the description, and those fields are first-write-wins, so a description reading "MTU 9000 to core" or "1Gbps uplink" overrides the device's real values into RCA and LLM evidence.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The capture's terminal metadata write reuses the same context that bounds the device work, so on the Postgres backend a timed-out capture never records its failure and the row stays `running` forever. The success path can also discard the sealed blob for the same reason. `cleanup()` builds its own context precisely for this.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: Dial, handshake and exec are attempted once, so one reset costs a whole capture interval and writes a failure row. The command is a read-only `show running-config` inside a 60 s budget with a 10 s dial timeout, so retries would fit.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: Junos uptime is cut at `" users"`, and FreeBSD prints `" user"` for a single session (often the collector's own), so `Uptime` comes back as "10 days, 2:31, 1 user, load averages: 0.10, 0.15". The fixture writes the impossible "1 users".

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The IOS-XR BGP-summary binding requires a BGP version in column 1, but XR prints a speaker id there, so every XR row is refused and the typed binding is dead. Fails closed to the regex analyzer.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The IOS-XR syslog binding requires a three-part tag; XR emits four parts, so every XR log line is dropped. Reproduced through the real parser.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The catch-all arm returns store and database errors as 400 with `err.Error()` verbatim, so a pgx SQLSTATE or a server path reaches the caller and no error is logged. `handleList` does the opposite in the same file. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The filter length bound is checked on the raw text but re-checked on the canonical rendering, which inserts spaces around parentheses. A 246-character filter is accepted with 202 and then fails in the runtime naming a length the operator never wrote. Verified by probe.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The `ActiveFor` error is consumed only as `aerr == nil && found`, so a store read failure silently disables the durable one-capture-per-device gate with no log. The in-process claim covers it while the process lives.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: No test constructs `pcap.SSHGateway`: the host-key fail-closed decision, the mismatch refusal and the SCP length-prefixed allocation bound are all unexercised. `internal/configstore/sshgw_test.go` is the harness that should have been reused.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: Same gap on the other live SSH gateway, including the new streaming path and its 128 MB cap, which exists nowhere else.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The deferred `FinishedAt` stamp writes to a local after the unnamed result has been copied, so every collected `DeviceState` carries the zero time. Only the never-ran path is correct. No consumer reads it today. (both lenses)

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: An over-long line is flushed through `writeLine`, which prepends a newline separator, so a >64 KiB device line reaches the bundle split by newlines the device never printed. The file's header claims byte-identity with the buffered pass.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `cancelPendingLocked` discards `Stop()`'s result, so an already-fired timer blocked on the mutex disarms the arm that replaced it, while the API reports it armed. Reproduced (10,240 of 20,000 re-arms wiped with a 1 ns window).

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `os_version_pattern` is compiled but not required to have a capture group, while `ResolveOS` indexes `m[1]` unconditionally. A groupless pattern loads and panics on the first matching sysDescr. Not reachable from runtime input: the profiles are embedded, review-gated data.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The dialect-versus-vendor id collision check runs in one direction only, so whichever document loads second silently overwrites the capture command and unions both families' volatile rules.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `validateIdentityProbe` applies the forbidden-byte list only: no read-only verb requirement and no control-character sweep, both of which the capture and verify validators enforce on commands run at the same devices. `capture.show_version_cmd` gets no validation at all.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: The monitoring ceiling gate is keyed on the raw cache id rather than the deduped canonical device, so a second source reporting an already-monitored device is charged again. At a hard Community ceiling the refusal switches the whole device off for one poll interval with a false "licence ceiling full" reason.

subsystem: 3.5 Device access: config store, capture, protocol diagnostics, parsers
what: `enrichVendors` writes `OSVersion` from sysDescr without `OSVersionSource`/`OSVersionAt`, so `osprobe.Plan` returns no rungs and the version ladder is locked out. Permanent for store-seeded rows, wiped each poll for source-owned ones.

`Observe` treats "absent from the overage list" as "the episode ended", but `State.Overages` omits a ceiling both when it is within limit and when it was not measured. One failed watched-prefix read during a live overage therefore deletes the durable `overage_since` from disk and restarts it at `now`. That timestamp is the one fact the register exists to keep.

The new `FeatureMSPManagement` gate is on `POST /api/orgs` only. `POST /api/onboard` creates an org and a tenant in one call with no entitlement check, so the paid capability is fully usable on a Community licence.
The "second real tenant needs MSP" gate counts and then creates outside any lock, with no ceiling check in the store, so two concurrent creates can both take the last slot.

`/metrics` calls `licenceUsage`, which reaches `bgpWatch.List` and `pool.Begin` with only the scrape's request context bounding it. A pool-acquire stall therefore blocks the scrape that carries the alert-delivery heartbeat and the engine-liveness counters. Server-side statement and lock timeouts cap the query itself.

The usage sparkline builds its path with a moveto test that is true on every iteration, so every point is a new subpath and the Trend column paints nothing, while the SVG still advertises a peak to a screen reader.

`handleTenantIdPPut` rebuilds the whole `ssoidp.Config` from a body that has no `kind` or `elevation`, and `Set` full-replaces the record, so a tenant admin toggling a tenant-bound ELEVATION connection silently converts it to a standing one. Every subsequent sign-in then provisions accounts and grants permanent roles instead of a time-bound binding, with nothing in the response, the audit detail or the log saying the access model changed.

The End button on elevated access does `.catch(() => {}).finally(clear)`, so a failed `DELETE /api/auth/elevation` removes the row and closes the menu exactly as success does. The operator believes they stepped down while the grant is still live and no revocation was audited.

The Postgres platform-trail floor matches mutating method plus path prefix but omits `platformPathExclusions`, so login, refresh, copilot and webhook rows are kept for the platform horizon instead of the configured retention. Over-retention, not loss.

The elevation grant is persisted before `enforceConcurrentLoginDeny` and `mintSession`, and neither failure path removes it. Since elevation resolves by principal id, a sign-in the server reported as failed can leave live elevated access attached to the next ordinary session.

`completeElevationSSO` still redirects to the generic post-login path while the standing and failure paths became locator-aware in the same change, so a per-tenant elevation sign-in lands off the tenant's own entry point. Cosmetic: the token fragment is still consumed.

With no locator candidate, `providerVisible` passes every alias, so the public sign-in page enumerates every tenant-bound IdP by alias and display name, and offers buttons whose per-tenant callback always refuses. Documented and test-pinned as today's behaviour, which is why it is low rather than a finding against the code.

A failed `api.permissions()` read is mapped to an empty grid with no error, so the API-key wizard shows "Checking which scopes your role may issue" forever while still allowing the key to be minted with a default scope set the operator never saw. The server re-authorises every scope, so nothing escalates.

A transient probe failure is recorded as a permanent `Verified: false` verdict for that snapshot, and `ProbeTick` then skips any snapshot it has a verdict for, so nothing ever re-probes it. The restorability alert stays lit, the coverage view shows a failed verify that never ran, and the rule's own 15-minute grace for a transient failure is defeated. Manual verify clears it; the daily snapshot displaces the key.

Under `set -euo pipefail`, the busy-port message builds a suffix in a command substitution ending in `[ -n "$var" ] && printf`, which exits 1 for the two entries with no mover variable (514/tcp, 514/udp). The assignment therefore aborts the installer before `die` prints anything. Reproduced: a host rsyslog on 514 kills a fresh install with no diagnostic, which is exactly the case the check was added to report.

`Put` updates memory under the lock and writes the file outside it, and every caller does an unsynchronised read-modify-write, so two concurrent platform-admin writes can leave disk holding the older config, including the deliberate snapshot-schedule stop the bootstrap reads.

The cleanup defer deletes the temp index unconditionally, and OpenSearch answers 404 when the restore never created it, so the commonest failure path reports a phantom leaked index, taints the verdict detail and logs an ERROR.

`ProbeTick` calls the probe directly, bypassing the single operation slot every operator-initiated snapshot action takes, so a scheduled restore can collide with a manual delete on the same repository and is invisible in `GET /operations`.

The 200-index cap bounds only a client-supplied list; an `in_place` restore with no list materialises the snapshot's whole index set and comma-joins it into the request line, which exceeds OpenSearch's 4 kB initial-line limit past roughly 130 daily indices. The failure message then claims the indices were left closed when nothing was closed.

All eleven new rollbacks drop their tables without deleting the `schema_migrations` row, so the migration never re-applies and the API boots healthy against a missing table. This is the repo's dominant existing convention (27 of 48 migrations have no rollback at all), and `0023`/`0024` are the two that do it right.

The OpenSearch collectors dial `https://localhost:9200` and CA-verify, but the OpenSearch SVID carries only `DNS:opensearch`, so both search-tier collectors fail on TLS installs. `stack-watchdog.sh` fixed exactly this in the same commit and the ClickHouse probe in the same file already uses the service name. Loud failure (MANIFEST rows plus exit 2).

Under `set -eu`, three new bare `X=$(curl ...)` assignments abort the script on a transport error, so the fallback branch written directly beneath line 274 is dead. Same pattern as five pre-existing assignments, and the abort is caught by `deploy-qualify.sh` and the watchdog.

`MarkNotified` files under the tenant derived at fire time; `Clear` re-derives it at resolve time. When the device was deleted or re-tenanted in between, the clear targets a different key and the record survives, so every restart within the 7-day window re-emits a resolve event for an alert that ended long ago.

The second snapshot repository's single-writer guard is one exact string compare against one hard-coded path, and does not consult the repository listing it already fetched. A trailing slash defeats both that guard and the netops-fs one, and OpenSearch happily resolves two names onto one blob tree.

`release-manifest` stamps `status: verified`, `method: git-retained+sha256` and a measured digest on a git-retained artifact on the strength of `os.path.isfile`. `release_fetch` does re-hash the same copy, which is why the asymmetry is a defect.

`--require-archive` gates on `entries[0]` while `archive_statuses` records every artifact, so an unarchived secondary (distro-packaging) artifact would pass. Latent: every current pin carries `retained_in_git`.

`run_oneshot` records a ledger row on failure only, and B3 has no follow-up `record`, so a successful `opensearch-init` ISM bootstrap produces no verdict. A passing B3 is indistinguishable from one that never ran.

subsystem: 3.9 Platform plumbing: pipeline debug, alert delivery, metrics, query

The tracker-195 truncation ladder drops the ranking tail (rung B) before the `grounding_context.path_graph` block (rung C). The Health and Routing lanes take `scope.device` in their dependency array but never put it into the PromQL, so both run fleet-wide. The three lanes that can scope do.

The timeline read shares the object read's fatal handler, so a timeline-only failure paints "This case could not be loaded." above a fully populated answer card. The comment two lines above says only the object read is fatal.

`BundlePolicyForm` never calls `onReload` after a save, so the retention hint keeps quoting the mount-time stored value and can tell the operator "Saving keeps 7" when the platform keeps 14. The snapshot form does reload.
"Open in Cloud" navigates to Infrastructure, Applications, Catalog. The nav split moved the href and left the label.

A raw NUL byte is used as the map-key separator instead of the escape, so git classifies the whole 6.7 KB new file as binary: undiffable, unblameable, unmergeable and invisible to grep. `ExperienceOverview.tsx:437` has the same byte past the 8 KB sniff window.
`not_declared` is not a key in `REASON_TEXT`, so the raw enum token is printed to the operator in the slot the file reserves for a sentence. Every sibling reason is present.

Any poll error rewrites the row's status to `failed` purely to stop the polling effect, and nothing re-reads it, so one 502 permanently shows a running capture as Failed and hides the download for the file that did complete.

The measuring layout effect has empty deps and bails when the ref is null, and the empty-state branch carries no ref, so a list that mounts empty and fills in later renders only its overscan. The device inventory does exactly that on a fresh install.

On any read failure that is not 501/503 the list is set to `[]` and the render falls through to a definitive empty state ("This tenant has declared no overrides"), so the screen asserts the failure and "nothing exists" at the same time.

`route()` redacts all-digit segments and 8+ character hex runs only, so short ids (including the docstring's own `/orders/1f9c/pay` example) and usernames reach the stored `route` label. The backend clips it and never scrubs it.

`post()` handles 503 only. A 400 (which a custom cohort key produces, since the server decodes with `DisallowUnknownFields`) or a 401 destroys the already-spliced batch with no console output and no backoff, forever, so the installer cannot tell a healthy app from a broken key.

`cloudStatus === "error"` is surfaced only inside the cloud domain's empty state, but the same change merges the cloud read into every domain and renames the default one "All networks, the whole discovered estate". A failed cloud read therefore draws the on-prem fabric with no warning.
